idea.sentence: Visitors come for one doorway, so the club is seen three times, each view larger and nearer, climbing a stair from a common floor until the green doors fill the last square.

notes: The stair works: three views share a floor at the bottom of row 12, and they climb 2, 4 and 6 rows across columns 1–2, 3–6 and 7–12. The last step does not make the green doors fill the square, though. In view-3 the doors take only the lower third of rows 7–12, and the top two rows are wall and window. Crop view-3 tighter, about 4.5× and anchored low, so the doors and fanlight fill rows 8–12.

View-2 (columns 3–6, rows 9–12) and view-3 show almost the same framing of the same doorway, so the 'nearer' step reads as a repeat. Pull view-2 back to the whole corner, roof to pavement, so each step is a clear jump in distance.

View-1 is 2 columns by 2 rows, but its image fills only part of that cell, leaving a pale strip above it in row 11. Either fill columns 1–2 across rows 11–12 completely, or make it a true 2×2 square, so its top edge sits on a row line like the other two.

The doorway-cue label sits in row 6 above columns 7–8, a full row above view-3, which starts at row 7. It floats away from what it labels. Drop it to the last baseline of row 6, touching the top of view-3, or move it inside the photo's top-left module.

The lead sets four lines across columns 1–5 at a size close to the headline's counterweight, and the rag breaks awkwardly at 'St / Ignatius'. Rebreak it so 'St Ignatius Walk' stays on one line, or narrow it to columns 1–4 for a calmer rag.

The body ends in row 8. Rows 9–10 over columns 1–2 are empty above view-1, and that gap is good because it marks the bottom of the stair. Keep it empty, but align the body's last baseline to the bottom of row 8.
The headline spans columns 1–8 over rows 2–4, and the county label in columns 9–12 of row 2 balances it well. Columns 9–12 in rows 3–5 are left empty; that is fine and should stay.

Colour: the brown headline (#6F3F31) echoes the brick, and the olive lead (#353D20) is meant to echo the green doors. The olive reads near-black, though. Shift the accent toward the door green so the lead and the final doors connect.
critic.summary: The three views form a clear stair from a shared floor in row 12, and the headline block is confident. The payoff is weak: the last view does not fill with the green doors, view-2 nearly repeats view-3, and the doorway-cue floats a row above its photo. Recrop the last two views and seat the label on view-3.

copy.text: On the corner of St Ignatius Walk and Coronation Street, in the Ordsall area of Salford.
Established in 1903 as a purpose-built club for boys, it now welcomes people of both sexes. Visitors from around the world come on dedicated open days.

posters.title: Macclesfield — Ian Curtis

idea.sentence: Macclesfield in inscriptional capitals across the full width; beneath it, Ian Curtis and his memorial stone, with the stone listed at 1.2 km and marked on the Cheshire pin map in the one accent colour.

notes: Followed: Dan asked for images and a Trajan-like all-caps serif title. Both photos are added, the portrait in columns 1–5 and the stone in columns 6–12, and the headline is set in inscriptional capitals across columns 1–12. Fully done. The serif's echo of the carved stone letters is the strongest move on the page.

Headline: it spans 12 of 12 columns but stops short of the right margin by about a third of a column. Track it or scale it so the D lands on the column 12 edge, or make it clearly shorter and end it on column 11. As set it reads as near-miss, not intent.

Photo split: the portrait (columns 1–5, rows 3–9) and the stone (columns 6–12, rows 3–5) meet at the column 5/6 gutter with no visible module between them. The headline also sits tight on row 3, so the top half feels jammed. Drop both photos to begin on row 3's top baseline with a full baseline gap below the headline, and keep the 12 pt gutter readable.

Accent colour: the one accent is meant to tie the stone, its 1.2 km listing and its map pin together, but it is spread thin. The tiny 01/02 numerals in row 6 and the pin in rows 8–12 are the only carriers, and the pin sits mid-cluster without a label. Colour only the '01' and its 1.2 km figure, add a short 'Memorial Stone' tag beside the pin, and drop the accent from '02' so the link reads.

Column 6–8 text: the distances text is set in a 3-column measure at rows 8–9 and wraps badly ('(61 / km)'). Widen it to columns 6–9 or rewrite the break. Alternatively move it up to row 7 and fold the county label into it, freeing row 8.

Rows 6–9 under the stone: the list, label and distances stack in rows 6, 7 and 8 with uneven gaps; row 7 to 8 is visibly larger. Lock each item to the top baseline of its row, or group list and label in row 6 and leave row 7 as a deliberate empty module.

Lead paragraph: it spans columns 1–7 in rows 10–12 but sets only four lines starting mid-row 10, leaving row 12 mostly empty. Its size also competes with nothing. Either step it up so it fills rows 10–11 cleanly as the second voice after the headline, or narrow it to columns 1–5 to align with the portrait edge above.

Map: the pinfield spans columns 9–12 and rows 8–12, but the stray pins at left bleed toward column 8 and collide visually with the lead's measure. Clip or rescale the pin field so it stays inside columns 9–12, and give it a hairline frame or county outline so it reads as a map rather than noise.

Hierarchy: the eye goes headline, then portrait, then stone, then gets lost among four small text blocks on the right. Promote the stone entry (row 6) to a larger size so the stone photo, its name and its distance form one unit directly under the image.
critic.summary: Dan's request is met well. The inscriptional caps rhyme with the carved stone, and the two photos give the page real weight. The weaknesses are finishing on the grid. The headline falls short of column 12, the photos and headline crowd rows 2–3, the small right-hand text stack in rows 6–9 is unevenly spaced, and the accent fails to link the stone, its 1.2 km listing and the map pin as the idea promises. Tighten those links and the stack and this is a keeper.

posters.title: Battersea Power Station

idea.sentence: The station takes its name from Battersea, so the district's name spans the page beneath it, set just below the night-time Thames.

notes: Followed: the headline now sits in rows 9–10, in the bottom half beneath the photo, and the night-time Thames image is new. I can't confirm it differs from the earlier photo choice, but it reads as a fresh image. The request is done, so followed scores high.

The headline spans all 12 columns, and that carries the 'name spans the page' idea. Its descender-free baseline sits tight under the photo's bottom edge at row 8. Keep the full span, but hang the cap B optically so its stem aligns with the column 1 edge; it currently overhangs slightly to the left of the lead text.

The lead spans columns 1–8 in rows 11–12 at a large size, so each line breaks at only about 30 characters and the rag is uneven ('Theo' / 'Halliday'). Either narrow it to columns 1–6 at one size smaller, or keep 8 columns and reduce the size so the rag settles. Leave columns 9–12 of rows 11–12 empty as they are now.

The location caption in columns 1–3 sits at rows 7–8, but its first line floats mid-row. Drop it so its last baseline lands on the photo's bottom edge at row 8, and its foot shares a line with the image.
The kicker in column 1–3, row 2 aligns its cap height with the photo top, which is good. Rows 3–6 of columns 1–3 stay empty, an intentional void that lets the photo lean right. Keep it.
Color: #814824 picks up the brick and sodium lights in the photo, so the accent, the photo and the warm-grey paper work as one. No change needed.
critic.summary: This version follows Dan: the title moves to the bottom half and the photo is new. The 12-column headline under a 9-column photo makes the idea legible. Remaining fixes are small: tighten the lead's measure and rag in columns 1–8, align the caption's foot to the bottom of row 8, and optically align the B to column 1.

idea.sentence: Bamburgh sits on the far northeast coast of England, so the photo and its county caption form one block in the top-right modules, and the open field to the left stands for the country below it.

notes: Idea: the top-right block of photo plus caption reads as 'northeast corner', but the empty field in columns 1–6, rows 2–7 does not register as 'the country' because nothing anchors it. Either drop a small locator (a map tick or the word ENGLAND) at column 1, row 7, or restate the idea as pure placement and keep the field empty with conviction.
Grid: the photo spans columns 7–12 and rows 2–6, and the caption hangs one row below it on column 7. That is a clean, intentional corner block; keep it.

Grid: the body sits at columns 7–11 in rows 11–12 and repeats the column-7 axis. Row 10 is left as a single empty row between the headline descender and the body, which feels like leftover rather than chosen space. Move the body up to start at row 10 so it locks under the 'g' descender, and leave rows 11–12 open as a deliberate bottom field.

Grid: the headline spans all 12 columns in rows 8–9, and the 'g' descender drops into row 10. Set the baseline of 'Bamburgh' on the bottom line of row 8 so the descender lands inside row 9 and does not crowd the body.

Hierarchy: the order is headline, then photo, then body, and it works. The caption in row 7 is too close in weight and size to the header row, though, so it reads as header furniture. Give it one step more size or tracking, or tie it tighter to the photo by placing it in the baseline directly under the image edge.

Type: the body measure across columns 7–11 gives about 40 characters, which is good. The rag is uneven, with a short 'the' line ending line 2. Rebreak so that line 2 does not end on an orphaned short word, or widen the body to column 12 to match the photo edge.

Type: the serif headline against the mono labels and the sans body is three voices. That is acceptable, but the mono caption and the sans body compete. Consider setting the caption in the same mono as the header and keeping the sans only for the body, which is what you have now, so keep that split consistent.

Colour: the #364314 headline echoes the grass in the bottom of the photo, which is a good link. Add the same green to one small element in the top-right block, such as the caption or a rule above it, so the accent ties the two blocks across rows 7–8.
critic.summary: A disciplined two-axis layout: the column-7 spine carries the photo, caption and body, and a full-width serif headline crosses it. The corner-block idea reads, but the open left field does not yet say 'England'. Tighten the vertical rhythm around the headline descender, decide what rows 10–12 are for, and give the caption more presence. It is close to keepable.

copy.text: Bamburgh Castle stands by the village of Bamburgh in Northumberland, on the northeast coast of England. It is a Grade I listed building; the village had a population of 414 at the 2011 census.

idea.sentence: Beachy Head is best understood by walking towards it, so three views step down and across the grid, each larger and closer, until the chalk face and lighthouse fill the lower right.

notes: The staircase reads: view-far spans 2 columns × 2 rows, view-middle 4 × 3, view-close 6 × 6. Each step moves right by exactly its own width (cols 1–2, 3–6, 7–12), so the walk is legible. Keep this progression. Tighten the middle step so the growth is even, for example 2×2 → 4×4 → 6×6, by extending view-middle to rows 4–7 and starting view-close at row 8.

View-middle (cols 3–6, rows 4–6) and the headline (cols 1–6, rows 7–10) share column 6 with only a baseline between them. The ascender of 'h' and the 'y' tail crowd the photo edge. Either start the headline one row lower, at rows 8–11, or end view-middle at row 5, so the photo and the headline do not collide.

Columns 7–12 in rows 4–6 are an empty block of 6 × 3 modules beside view-middle. This is good intentional air for the walk, but the lead in rows 2–3 then floats with nothing tying it down. Hang the lead from the top of row 2, aligned with the top edge of view-far. It currently starts about a baseline lower; correct that so the two share a hanging line.

Hierarchy: the headline at cols 1–6, rows 7–10 competes with view-close, which spans 6 × 6 on the right. The eye goes to the photo first, which suits the idea. However, the headline should then end the walk rather than interrupt it. Consider moving 'Beachy Head' to rows 2–4 across cols 7–12 in place of the lead, and dropping the lead to cols 1–5, rows 9–10, so the reading starts with the name and ends with the cliff.

Body text in cols 1–5, rows 11–12 has a rag that ends in the single orphan word 'Britain.' Set the measure to 4 columns (cols 1–4) or adjust the wrap so the last line carries at least two words. Also align the body baseline to the bottom of row 12 so it sits on the same line as the bottom of view-close.

Type: the lead is set too large and too close in size to body. Its three lines at roughly 2× body size in a 6-column measure feel like a second headline. Reduce it to about 1.5× body, or keep the size and narrow it to cols 7–11, so it reads as a step between the headline and the body.

Colour: the #C8102E accent appears only as the number frames on the three photos. Those frames are tiny, about a third of a column, and the red goes unnoticed. Either enlarge the numerals to a full 1-column module aligned to the bottom-left corner of each photo, or use the red once in type, for example on the lighthouse reference in the body. That way it echoes the red band of the lighthouse in view-middle and view-close.

Navy #012169 on the warm grey paper works with the cold sea tones in view-close. The far photo, however, is warmer and more saturated than the other two. Match its grade so the three steps read as one walk in one light.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea executed with a real stepped grid: 2-, 4- and 6-column photos marching down and right. The weak points are the headline colliding with view-middle at column 6 and a lead that competes with the body. The red accent is almost invisible, and the body rag ends in an orphan. Fix the vertical spacing between rows 6 and 7 and give the accent a real role, and this becomes a keeper.

posters.title: The Black Friar, City of London

idea.sentence: The City is the historic centre of London and the pub is one narrow wedge within it, so the City's name fills the page and The Black Friar sits beneath it.

notes: The city-name spans all 12 columns over rows 2–6, but LONDON runs nearly flush to the right margin while CITY OF stops short at about column 11. Track or size the headline so LONDON lands exactly on the column 12 edge. Leave CITY OF ragged short deliberately, so the two-line block reads as one measured slab.

The idea says the pub is 'one narrow wedge' within the City, yet the photo takes 7 of 12 columns and 6 rows. Wedge and slab end up competing. Cut the photo to columns 8–12 (5 columns) over rows 7–12. That leaves columns 5–7 as an empty channel, so the pub really reads as a sliver beneath the name.

Column 5 is the only empty column between text and photo, so the gutter reads as a gap rather than a decision. Widen it to two empty columns (5–6) or close it entirely. One lone module looks accidental.

Place-name 'The Black / Friar' at 4 columns sets two words per line with a heavy rag on line two. Extend it to columns 1–5, or drop one size so 'The Black Friar' breaks with a fuller second line. Keep its cap height on the row 8 hangline.

Body sits on rows 10–11 at columns 1–4 with five short lines and a ragged 'of London.' widow. Rebreak it to avoid the two-word last line. Align its last baseline to the bottom of row 11, or its first baseline to the top of row 10, so the text is anchored to a grid line rather than floating.

Row 12 in columns 1–5 is empty below the body while the photo runs to the bottom of row 12. That is fine as deliberate silence, but end the photo on row 11 or anchor the body to row 12 so the two columns share a common bottom edge.

The locator label in brown on row 7 matches the photo top, which is good. The rust accent on locator and place-name picks up the brick in the photo well. Keep it, but don't add the accent anywhere else.
critic.summary: A clear scale contrast that mostly delivers the idea: the full-width CITY OF LONDON slab dominates and the pub sits below. The photo is too large for a 'narrow wedge', and the single empty column 5 feels unresolved. Narrow the photo to about 5 columns, make the gap intentional, and tighten the rag in the place-name and body to bring this to a keeper.

copy.text: A Grade II* listed public house on Queen Victoria Street. The City, founded by the Romans as Londinium, is the historic centre of London.

idea.sentence: Bletchley Park lies about 50 miles north-west of London, so the photo takes the grid cell matching its place in England, with London one module diagonally south-east and the open page as territory.

notes: Idea: the map conceit is sound, but the geometry does not match the statement. The photo ends at column 10, row 10, while the london-marker sits at column 12, row 12. That puts London two modules diagonally away, not one. Move the london-marker to column 11, row 11 so it touches the photo's south-east corner exactly one module off.

Grid: the vector label spans columns 11–12 in row 11, which is the very module London should occupy. Once London moves to column 11, row 11, shrink the vector to a 1-column label at column 11, row 10, beside the photo's lower edge. That way the arrow points into London's cell rather than sitting on it.

Grid: the caption spans the photo's full 5 columns (6–10) but is only a short line. Keep it on row 11 but limit it to columns 6–8. This keeps column 11 clear for the London cell and makes it read as a caption, not a band.

Grid: the body (columns 1–4, rows 8–9) fills only about one and a half rows, then stops. Columns 1–5 in rows 10–12 are empty. That emptiness is the 'territory' and is good, but the body should start on the same baseline as the photo top in row 8. Check that its cap height aligns with the photo's top edge, not one baseline below it.

Grid: the north-tick at column 12, row 2 is the right instinct. To make the compass read as one system with the vector, align it to the same right edge as the london-marker in column 12, ending flush with the column edge.

Hierarchy: the order is headline (rows 2–4), lead (rows 6–7), then the photo. That is correct. But the lead spans 5 columns and the photo starts at column 6, so the two blocks touch edge to edge across a single gutter. Narrow the lead to columns 1–4 to match the body. That leaves column 5 as a clear empty module separating text from map.

Type: the headline at 7 of 12 columns over 3 rows is strong, and the serif/sans/mono pairing is clean. The lead's rag is good. The body's 4-column measure gives a slightly choppy rag, with 'penetrated the secret' falling short. Allow a soft rebreak, or widen to columns 1–4 plus a tighter tracking pass.

Type: the place-label in row 5 floats midway between headline and lead. Drop it to the top baseline of row 6 and push the lead down one baseline. This ties the label to the lead as its kicker instead of leaving it orphaned in its own row.

Color: the navy headline, and the red reserved for London alone, give a clear two-point story. But the red is only a 1-column, one-line label in row 12 and barely registers. Enlarge the dot to fill more of the column 11, row 11 cell, or set the vector arrow in red too. That links the photo to London in the accent colour.
Color: the photo's blue sky echoes the navy headline nicely. Keep the photo at its current scale; do not add any further colour.
critic.summary: A clean, well-typed poster with a worthwhile map idea. The grid does not yet prove that idea: London sits two modules from the photo instead of one, and the vector label occupies the cell London should own. Move London to column 11, row 11, tuck the vector into row 10, and pull the lead back to 4 columns. Then the composition would earn a keep.

copy.text: The principal centre of Allied code-breaking in the Second World War.
The estate housed the Government Code and Cypher School, which penetrated the secret communications of the Axis powers, most importantly the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers.

idea.sentence: The village is small and its county is large, so WILTSHIRE fills the width of the page while Castle Combe is a single small line and a single brown dot inside it.

notes: The idea depends on one brown dot, but in the pinfield (columns 7–12, rows 5–9) it sits beside three ringed markers at about column 9, row 8, and reads as one of four. Remove the rings, or turn them into plain grey dots, so the brown dot is the only accented mark in the field.

Nothing links CASTLE COMBE (columns 1–4, row 10) to its dot (column 9, row 8). Move the place-name to columns 7–10 in row 10, directly under the dot's column. Alternatively, run a hairline from the dot down to the top of row 10, so 'small line' and 'small dot' read as one statement.

The scattered dots at the bottom-left of the pinfield drift down into the gap between rows 9 and 10, near column 7, and crowd the top of the lead. Clip the pinfield to end at row 9 as specified, or drop those outliers.

WILTSHIRE spanning all 12 columns across rows 3–4 is correct and carries the idea. Keep it. Row 2, holding only the 3-column label, leaves a full empty row above it. Either keep that row as deliberate air or move the label onto the top baseline of row 3 and lift the headline by one row.

The lead in columns 7–12 (rows 10–11) is a large serif that visually outweighs CASTLE COMBE in columns 1–4. The hierarchy now runs WILTSHIRE → lead → place-name. Drop the lead one size step, to about 1.5× body, so the place-name becomes the second read after the county.

The body line sits alone in row 12, a full empty row below the lead and tight against the footer rule. Move it up to row 11, directly under the lead's last baseline. That frees row 12 as clean air above the footer.

The lead at 6 columns breaks at about 30 characters with a decent rag, but 'north-west of' hangs on line 1. Set the lead to columns 7–11 (5 of 12) so it breaks after 'miles', giving a tighter rag and one empty column at the right.

The parish caption in row 9 spans 6 columns but is only about 3 columns long. Set it to columns 1–3 so the caption's span matches its length; the remainder of row 9 under the photo then reads as an intentional empty module.
Colour works: the warm grey paper, the brown headline and dot matching the Cotswold stone, and the photo's blue sky as the only cool note. Keep the dot exactly in the headline brown.
critic.summary: A sound structure: a full-width county name over a half-and-half photo and pinfield, with text below. The core idea is undercut because the brown dot is not singular and has no visual tie to the CASTLE COMBE line. Rebalance the lead and the place-name, tighten rows 11–12, and clean up the pinfield so one dot carries the meaning.

copy.text: Around 5 miles north‑west of Chippenham and 10 miles north‑east of Bath.
At the 2021 census, the parish had a population of 356.

idea.sentence: The page stands for England, so Dan's Rosetta Stone photo sits low and to the right, in the cells where London lies.

notes: Idea: placing the photo low-right 'where London lies' on a map of England is a reasonable conceit, but nothing on the page signals the map. Either add a faint outline or locator dot in columns 8–12, rows 8–11, or let the photo's position be the only map cue and say so in the place-label in row 2.

The photo spans columns 8–11 and stops one column short of the right margin, while the place-label above runs 8–12. Extend the photo to columns 8–12 so both share the right edge, or pull the label back to 8–11. As it is, the right side has two different edges.

The photo occupies rows 8–11 and leaves rows 3–7 in columns 8–12 completely empty under a lone label. That 5×5 module void reads as accidental. Raise the photo to rows 6–11, a 6-row span, so it holds the right half. Or keep it at rows 8–11 and move the place-label down to row 7 so it heads the image.

The headline spans columns 1–7 and rows 2–4, but 'Museum' visibly overruns into column 8 toward the label's column. Set it a step smaller so it closes inside column 7, or let it run fully to column 8 and push the label to columns 9–12.

Lead (rows 5–6) and body (rows 7–8) stack directly, but the body starts one module lower than the lead's natural end, leaving a half-row gap. Start the body at row 7's top baseline, or move it to row 8 so the gap equals one full module.

Body ends in row 8 just as the photo begins in row 8, so the left column dies where the right one starts. Columns 1–7 in rows 9–12 are empty. Move the body down to rows 9–10 so the left text sits beside the photo and the two halves interlock diagonally.
The caption sits in row 12, one row below the photo's base in row 11. Move it to the first baseline under the photo, still within row 11 or at the top of 12, so it reads as attached.
Type: the lead at 5 columns gives a good 25–30 character measure and a clean rag. The body at the same 5 columns is fine. Keep the serif/grotesque pairing.

Color: the rust accent on the label and caption picks up the stone's ochre edge well. The photo is dark and low-contrast against the pale paper, though. Either crop tighter onto the inscribed face or brighten it a stop so it holds weight against the black headline.
critic.summary: A clean, competent page whose map idea isn't legible. The right half is mostly an unexplained void above a photo that misses the right margin by one column. To fix it, align the photo to columns 8–12, raise it or move the label down, and shift the body beside the photo so the left and right halves interlock.

copy.text: Established in 1753, the world's first public national museum.
Its permanent collection of eight million artefacts is the largest in the world. It documents the story of human culture from its beginnings to the present.

idea.sentence: A 55-metre figure is best understood by approaching it, so one aerial photo climbs a staircase of square-stepped frames, 2, 4 and 6 modules, standing on a shared bottom edge until the Giant fills the last.

notes: The idea is clear and the staircase reads at a glance. But the frames are not square: a 2-column by 2-row module is about 77 pt wide and 108 pt tall, so all three frames are portrait. Either drop 'square' from the idea, or keep the steps at 2, 4 and 6 columns and let the height follow the photo's ratio rather than the row count.

The magnifications (1×, 1.4×, 2×) do not track the frame spans (2, 4, 6 columns, which would be 1×, 2×, 3×). The Giant grows less than the frame does, so the approach feels uneven. Scale the crops 1×, 2× and 3× so the figure fills more of each step, as the idea promises.
The stepped void is the best grid move here: columns 1–6 rows 7–8 and columns 1–2 rows 9–10 stay empty and give the climb its shape. Keep it, and keep the shared bottom edge on row 12.

The status label sits in columns 1–4 and wraps, leaving 'MONUMENT' alone on a second line one baseline lower. The location label sits on a single line in columns 7–12. Widen the status label to columns 1–6 so both labels are one line on the same baseline in row 4.

The body (columns 1–4) and the lead (columns 7–12) are set at the same size. The left block is read first, but the right block is the real introduction. Swap them so the lead sits in columns 1–6 rows 5–6, or set the lead one step larger, so it is clear where reading starts after the headline.
The body measure in columns 1–4 is short, and columns 5–6 of rows 5–6 sit empty with no purpose. Extend the body to columns 1–5, or align its right edge to column 6 to echo photo-nearer below.

The headline spans 12 columns but its longest line ends near column 8. Either state the span as 1–8, or set it larger so 'Cerne Abbas' reaches column 10 or 11 and the top of the page carries more weight against the large photo in rows 7–12.

The number badges in the photo corners use a serif face, which clashes with the sans and mono pairing. Set them in the mono used for the labels, at label size, and inset them one baseline from the frame corners.
Colour works: the dark green mono labels pick up the turf, and the warm grey paper lets the photo carry the only saturated area. Keep it.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea with a strong stepped void and a shared baseline for the photos. To reach a keepable 7, fix three things: the frames are not square as claimed, the zoom levels lag behind the frame spans, and the text blocks above are flat in hierarchy with unequal label spans.

copy.text: Shallow trenches cut into the turf and backfilled with chalk rubble.
A hill figure 55 metres long, near the village of Cerne Abbas in the Cerne Valley, Dorset Downs.

idea.sentence: Crawley has no single landmark, so its name takes the full width of the page and the town's square, its place on the map and its county hang from it.

notes: Row 12 and most of row 11 sit empty across all 12 columns, so the stack reads as top-heavy rather than hanging from the name. Either move county-name and county-note down one row to rows 11–12, or open the gap between town-name and the photo so the content fills rows 5–12 deliberately.

Column 8 is left empty as a gutter module between the photo (cols 1–7) and the map (cols 9–12). That works, but the population label and county-name also stop at column 7 while their companions start at 9. Keep this two-zone split consistent: make the photo span cols 1–8, or start the right zone at column 8, so the empty module reads as a decision.

The pin-map fills rows 5–7, but its dots cluster in the lower half and the red pin floats near column 11. Crop or scale the pinfield so it fills the full 3-row block and its bottom edge aligns with the photo's bottom in row 8. The distances text then hangs from that shared edge instead of sitting mid-row.

Distances sits at the top of row 8 while the photo runs to the bottom of row 8, and the population label drops into row 9. Move distances to row 9 so it shares a baseline with population. The two captions will then form one line across columns 1–12.

County-name sits in row 10 at roughly a third of the town-name cap height, and in red. It competes with CRAWLEY as a second headline. Keep it at 7 columns but drop it to about half its current size, or set it in the label style. The county is meant to hang from the name, not rival it.

County-note is set in grey, smaller and lighter than distances, in the same 4-column measure. Match it to the distances text in size and colour so the right column reads as one voice. Hang its first baseline on the county-name cap line in row 10, not slightly below it.

The red in the map pin and the red county-name tie together well. Add no further red elsewhere. Consider tinting the target ring and pin a single red with no outline duplicate so the accent stays one clean mark.
critic.summary: A clear idea executed with a confident full-width name across 12 columns. The lower half loses grid discipline: empty rows 11–12 feel unplanned, the captions in rows 8–9 don't align, and the red county headline competes with CRAWLEY. Tighten the column 8 split, align the captions and drop the county to a supporting level.

idea.sentence: Goonhilly lies at the far south-western tip of England, so its photo sits in the bottom-left corner of the grid.

notes: The stated idea (photo in the bottom-left corner as the south-west tip) works only if the reader reads the page as a map, and the pinfield in columns 9–12, rows 10–12 also puts the Goonhilly dot at its own bottom-left. Two competing maps weaken both. Either move the pinfield into columns 6–8, rows 10–12 so it reads as a legend for the photo, or drop the pins and let the photo carry the idea alone.

The place-label floats in row 6 with an empty module above it and no relation to the lead's first line. Drop it to the last baseline of row 6 so it sits directly on 'Cornwall' in row 7. Or align it to the lead's first baseline in row 5 so the two columns start together.

'Cornwall' in row 7 sits flush on the photo's top edge in row 8 with no breathing room, while the gap between the headline and the lead in row 5 is generous. Keep 'Cornwall' and the photo but leave one baseline of clearance. Or shrink 'Cornwall' to the lead's size, since a second blue headline at about 30% of the main headline's size competes for second place in the hierarchy.

The body in columns 7–12 runs 6 columns at about 11 pt, which gives roughly 80 characters per line, too long. Narrow it to columns 7–11 (5 of 12), or set it at 12–13 pt on the baseline, so the measure drops to about 60 characters.

Columns 7–12, rows 9–10 sit empty between the body and the pinfield, while the photo column is packed from row 6 to row 12. That reads as leftover space rather than an intended empty module. Pull the pinfield up to rows 9–12, or push the body down to row 9 so it aligns with the photo's midpoint.

Column 6 is an empty gutter column running the full height, which is good, but the photo stops at column 5 while the lead and body begin at column 7. Keep that relationship consistent: extend the place-label and 'Cornwall' to stop exactly at the photo's right edge, which they currently do; this part is fine.

The blue accent appears on 'Cornwall', on the Goonhilly pin, and in the photo's sky, and that ties the page together well. Make the pin's blue exactly match the type blue so the link reads as deliberate.
critic.summary: A clean, well-set poster with a strong full-width headline and a sensible two-zone split at column 6. The bottom-left photo idea is legible but diluted by a second map, the pinfield, which makes the same point in a different corner. Tighten the left stack (label, county, photo), shorten the body measure, and resolve the empty modules in columns 7–12, rows 9–10. That would bring it to a keeper.

idea.sentence: Dan's single photograph of the Blackbird rewards a longer look, so it appears three times, each larger than the last, stepping across the grid towards the viewer.

notes: The three photos share a top edge at row 5 and grow 2→3→5 columns and 2→3→5 rows, which reads as a progression. The 'stepping towards the viewer' idea needs a staircase, though. Drop the medium photo to start on row 6 and the large one on row 7, or anchor all three to a common bottom edge on row 9, so each step moves down as well as across.

The large photo ends at column 10, leaving columns 11–12 empty beside it. That empty band looks accidental. Either extend the large photo to columns 6–12 (7 of 12, keeping the 2→3→5→7 rhythm), or give columns 11–12 a purpose by placing the place/county labels there, ranged to the photo's top edge.

Each photo starts on a column edge (1, 3, 6), but the gutters between them are not consistent. Small to medium is one gutter; medium to large is a gutter plus some slack. Snap the medium photo to columns 3–5 exactly and the large photo to columns 6–10 so every gap equals one 12 pt gutter.
The numbered boxes 1–3 sit at different offsets inside each frame. Place each one at the same distance from its photo's bottom-left corner, one baseline in, so the numbers form a repeating mark.

The lead sits in rows 10–11 directly under the small and medium photos, but the large photo dominates the eye on columns 6–10. Narrow the lead to columns 1–5 so its rag clears the large photo's left edge at column 6. Its lines then end inside the measure instead of drifting toward the image.

The body line in row 12 floats a full row below the lead, and the gap reads as missing content. Move it up into row 11 directly under the lead, on the next baseline after a one-line space. That frees row 12 as a deliberate empty band above the footer.

The headline spans all 12 columns but stops short of column 12's right edge, by about half a column. Track it or scale it so the 'd' ends exactly on the right margin. Otherwise reduce it to a clear 10-column span. A near-miss span is the weakest choice.

Red is used only on the place label in row 4. Repeat the accent once, on the number box of photo 3 or a hairline under the large photo. The accent then ties the label to the image that names it, and it echoes the red serial on the aircraft's tail.
critic.summary: The repeated-photo idea is good, and the 2/3/5 Fibonacci spans are a real grid decision. Right now, though, the photos only step sideways, not toward the viewer. Columns 11–12 beside the large photo and row 12 under the body text feel leftover rather than designed. Stagger or bottom-align the photos, resolve the right-hand columns, tighten the text stack, and snap the headline to a true span to make this keepable.

idea.sentence: The bunker hides beneath a modest bungalow while the county around it is large, so ESSEX fills the page and the place sits small inside it.

notes: The idea says the place sits small inside a large county, but ESSEX only spans rows 2–4 while the photo, lead and pinfield compete below it. To make the county feel like it holds the place, either push ESSEX to rows 2–5 or set the photo smaller (columns 1–3, rows 6–8) so the size contrast is the message.

The pinfield is assigned columns 5–12, rows 9–12, but the dots cluster in columns 8–10 with a stray pair drifting into columns 7–8 at row 12. Either scale the map to really fill its 8-column field or reassign it to columns 7–12 so the empty modules in columns 5–6 read as intent rather than leftover.

Columns 5–8 sit empty from row 5 to row 8 between the photo and the lead. That is a good empty field, but nothing answers it. Keep it open and align the pinfield's left edge to column 5 so the void has a firm boundary below.

The lead in columns 9–12, rows 6–7 is the second voice, yet it starts a full row below the place-label and floats. Snap the label to the top of row 5 to match the photo top, and start the lead on the first baseline of row 6 so the right stack hangs from the same line as the photo.

The body in columns 1–4, rows 9–10 runs about 40 characters per line with a ragged right that is fine. However, it sits directly under the photo with no gap module. Start it one baseline lower inside row 9 so the caption relationship is clear.

The distance-label in row 11, columns 1–4, is orphaned between the body and the footer. Move it to row 12 so it aligns with the pinfield's bottom and reads as the map's caption, or move it into columns 5–8 at row 12 next to the dots.
The ESSEX headline overshoots column 12 on the X and starts left of column 1 on the E's optical edge. Track or scale it so the stems sit exactly on the column 1 and column 12 edges.
Olive on near-black works, and the single accent dot ties the map to the headline. Keep the place-label in the accent, but drop the photo's saturation slightly so its greens don't fight the olive.
critic.summary: A bold, legible poster: the 12-column ESSEX and the olive accent dot carry the idea. The middle band and the lower right are loose, though. The pinfield underuses its 8-column field, the lead floats a row below its label, and the distance-label is orphaned in row 11. Tighten the alignments to rows 5 and 12, and sharpen the size contrast between county and place.

idea.sentence: The page stands for England with north at the top, so the photo of Keswick sits high and to the west, its lower-right corner on column 5, row 4, where the town falls on the map.

notes: The map conceit is clever, but nothing on the page tells the reader where England's outline would sit. Put a hairline or faint coordinate tick at the column 5 / row 4 corner, or set the map-key label against that corner. That makes 'north up' legible rather than a private rule.

The photo occupies only 4 columns × 2 rows and reads as a thumbnail floating in rows 3–4. Columns 6–8 and row 5 sit empty and inert between it and the body text. Either extend the photo leftward to start at column 1, keeping the corner fixed at column 5 / row 4 so the idea holds, or move the keswick-body to columns 7–10 so the gap becomes a single deliberate module rather than three dead columns.

Row 5 is entirely empty, and the county-label in row 6 floats above the headline. Move the county-label to the top of row 7, directly above the cap height of 'Lake'. Leave row 6 as the clean break between the map zone (rows 2–5) and the title zone (rows 7–12).

The headline 'Lake / District' spans 8 columns, but 'Lake' ends near column 5 while 'District' runs to column 8, so the ragged right block feels unanchored. Size it so 'District' fills exactly columns 1–8. Optically align the L stem to the column 1 edge; it currently sits slightly inside the margin, compared with the county-label and lead.

The also-known label in columns 9–12, row 10 hangs off the baseline of 'District' and works well. Snap it precisely to the headline baseline in row 10, not floating above it, so the two read as one line across 12 columns.

The lead spans columns 1–6 in rows 11–12 at a good 3-line rag. Columns 7–12 of rows 11–12 are empty. That is acceptable, but consider pulling the lead to columns 1–5 so its right edge echoes the photo's corner at column 5. This repeats the key vertical of the idea.

The olive accent is used on the photo-label and also-known, but the photo's warm orange boats compete with it. Either shift the accent toward the photo's lake blue-green, or restrict the accent to the photo-label alone so it marks Keswick, the map point, only.

Keswick-body sits at roughly 12 pt with ~30-character lines across 4 columns. This is fine, but its top should align to the photo's top edge on the row 3 hangline; it currently sits a few points lower. Fix it to the same baseline.
critic.summary: A clean, competent page with a genuinely interesting map-as-grid idea. The idea is barely signalled, though, and the upper half has too much undifferentiated empty space: the small photo, empty columns 6–8, and dead row 5. Enlarge or anchor the photo around the column 5 / row 4 corner, tighten the label-to-headline relationship, and align the headline width to its 8-column span.

copy.text: Keswick, a market town, lies within the national park just north of Derwentwater. Bassenthwaite Lake is 4 mi away.
A mountainous region and national park, famous for its lakes and mountains.

idea.sentence: The hill is small and flat-topped; the county around it is large, so SOMERSET spans the full width and the hillfort sits low beneath a field of open paper.

notes: The headline 'SOMERSET' spans 12 of 12 columns and rows 2–4. Its cap height fills roughly 2.5 rows and leaves dead space inside row 4. Either scale it so the caps run exactly from the top of row 2 to the foot of row 4, or crop it to rows 2–3. The baseline should land on a row line, not float.
The open field covers rows 5–7, three empty rows across all 12 columns, and it carries the idea well. Keep it. Do not let anything creep into it.

The photo spans columns 1–5 and rows 8–12, but its left edge appears to sit slightly inside column 1 while the headline's S overshoots it. Optically align the S's left edge to the column 1 line so the image and the headline share one vertical.

Column 6 is an empty gutter column between the photo and the text block. That works. But the lead and the label start at column 7, while the footer's COUNTRY item also starts at column 7 and COUNTY at column 3. Keep the footer as fixed, and make sure the lead's left edge sits exactly on the column 7 line it shares with the footer.

The lead spans 6 columns, rows 9–10, and leaves a gap between the label in row 8 and the lead's first line. Move the lead up so its cap height hangs from the top of row 9 on the baseline grid. At present the first line sits about one baseline low.

The body spans columns 7–11 at roughly 50 characters per line, which is fine. Its last line, 'Beauty.', makes a single-word widow. Rebreak the text or narrow the span to columns 7–10 so the rag ends on 2+ words. Also bottom-align the body's last baseline with the foot of the photo at row 12.

Type pairing uses mono for the label and a serif for the lead and body under a grotesk headline. That is three families. Consider setting the lead in the headline grotesk at a lighter weight to cut back to two voices.

The olive headline colour is repeated only in the small row 8 label, and the photo's saturated blue sky and green grass fight the muted olive. Either pull the olive into a thin rule at the top of row 8 across columns 7–12, or desaturate the photo slightly so the olive stays the single accent.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea, executed with a confident full-width headline and three honest empty rows. To reach 'keep' quality across the board, the poster needs tighter baseline alignment of the headline and lead to row lines, a fix for the widow in the body, one fewer typeface, and a better link between the olive accent and the photo.

idea.sentence: Liverpool lies in England's north-west, so its photo sits where the city falls on a map of the country, with the Irish Sea to its west and London far to the south-east.

notes: The map idea only half reads. The photo at columns 3–7, rows 5–7 sits correctly in the upper-left (north-west) quadrant. But the lead and body fill columns 3–8 across rows 9–12, so the 'south' of the map is mostly text, and the London label at columns 9–12 reads as a side caption to the lead rather than a distant point. Narrow the lead and body to columns 3–7 so column 8 stays empty as a buffer. Then drop the London label to row 12, columns 10–12, so it becomes the farthest south-east point on the page.

The region label at columns 9–12, row 12 currently occupies London's territory and reads as a second south-east place, which muddles the map. The city region surrounds Liverpool, so move this label next to the photo: columns 8–10, row 7, hanging from the photo's bottom edge. This frees row 12 on the right for London alone.

The photo is too weak for the image that carries the idea. Its 5×3 block sits under a 10-column headline, and row 8 is left as a dead empty band below it. Extend the photo to rows 5–8 (4 of 13). It still sits in the north-west quadrant and closes the gap above the lead.

The Irish Sea label is right-aligned to the edge of column 2 and centred on row 6, against the photo's middle. Keep it exactly there; it is the clearest map move on the page. Consider giving the label two lines within columns 1–2 so it reads as an area rather than a caption.

Headline: the descender of the 'p' in columns 7–8 nearly touches the county label in row 4. Set the label on the last baseline of row 4 rather than the first so a clear baseline separates them. Keep the 10-column span; the left-edge alignment at column 3 with the photo, lead and body is good.

Body copy: the second line '507,915 in 2025.' is a short stub across a 6-column measure. Narrowing the body to columns 3–7 will rebreak it into two more even lines. Hold the body to the same left edge and to row 11's first baseline.

Colour: red appears only on the county label in row 4, while the warm paper and grey photo sit quietly. The bunting in the photo already carries red, so set the London label in the same red. The two places on the map would then be linked by colour, with the Irish Sea label kept grey as geography.
critic.summary: A clean start: there is a strong 10-column headline and a consistent column-3 axis, and the Irish Sea label is placed with intent. The map conceit is diluted, though. Text blocks occupy the 'south' of the page, and the region label competes with London in the lower right. The photo is also undersized for the image that carries the idea. Enlarge the photo to rows 5–8. Pull the lead and body back to columns 3–7. Move the region label beside the photo and push London alone to the bottom-right corner in red.

idea.sentence: Merstham is a small town in Surrey, just beyond the Greater London border, so the county name fills the page and the town hangs beneath it as the second level.

notes: The county headline spans 12 of 12 columns across rows 2–3 and reads as the page. Keep it, but trim the tracking so the S sits flush to the column 1 edge. Right now the optical overhang makes the left edge drift from the photo and from MERSTHAM below.

The photo spans columns 1–8 in rows 4–6 and butts almost directly under SURREY with no breathing baseline. Add one baseline of space above it so it rests on the row 4 line rather than touching the descenders of the headline row.

MERSTHAM spans columns 1–8 in rows 7–8 but its set width stops short of the photo's right edge at column 8. Either size it up to end exactly at column 8 so the town locks to the image block, or drop it to columns 1–6 and make the difference clearly intentional.
The pinfield in columns 9–12, rows 4–8 bleeds stray dots into column 8 at row 8, beside the end of MERSTHAM. Clip the field to columns 9–12 so the red pin owns that right-hand stack.
Move the red pin dot level with the MERSTHAM cap height in row 7–8. The town name and its location then share one horizontal, and the map explains the word.

The borough label sits alone in row 9 with rows 9–10 otherwise empty, so it floats. Move it up to sit one baseline under MERSTHAM at the top of row 9. The empty module rows 9–10 then read as a deliberate pause before the lead.

The lead spans columns 1–7 in rows 11–12 at a size that gives about 30 characters per line with a clean rag. Keep it. Align its first baseline with the body's first baseline in columns 9–12; they currently start on different lines.
The body in columns 9–12 is set small and tight, with lines near 40 characters. Open its leading to the 12 pt baseline so its three lines sit on the grid alongside the lead.
Red is used only for SURREY and the pin, which correctly ties county to place. The photo's red phone boxes in the bottom of rows 5–6 echo the accent. Keep the palette as is.
critic.summary: The idea is clear and the scale contrast between SURREY across all 12 columns and MERSTHAM in columns 1–8 does the work. The weaknesses are in alignment. SURREY's edge drifts optically, MERSTHAM falls short of the column 8 photo edge, pinfield dots stray into column 8, and the lead and body don't share a first baseline in rows 11–12. Tighten these and the poster is keepable.

idea.sentence: Newcastle sits high in the north-east of England, so its photo sits high on the right of the grid, in the cell where the city falls on the map.

notes: The idea is not shown on the page. The pinfield occupies only columns 1–4, rows 3–6, so its green Newcastle dot falls near column 4, row 3. The photo spans columns 7–12, rows 3–6, which is half the width and a third of the height. That is not 'the cell where the city falls'. Scale the pinfield up to the whole live area as a faint underlay (columns 1–12, rows 2–11), then let the dot's position decide the photo's cell.

Shrink the photo to a true north-east cell, for example columns 9–12, rows 2–4 (4 of 12 columns, 3 rows). Its top-left corner should touch the Newcastle dot. At 6×4 modules it reads as the generic 'image goes top right' slot and not as a map coordinate.

Columns 5–6, rows 3–6 form a dead two-column channel. The pinfield also floats inside its four modules, with the lowest pin dropping to row 6 and no clear edge. Either extend the map across that channel or align the pinfield's outer pins to the column 1 and column 4 edges so the block reads as a placed unit.

The grid-note in columns 7–12, row 7 explains what the layout should be showing. Once the photo sits on the dot, delete the note, or move it into a single column beside the dot as a 1-row caption. That frees row 7 as a clean empty band above the headline.

The headline spans columns 1–10 over rows 8–11 and is the clear first read; keep it. The descender of 'upon' pushes toward row 12, so set the second line one baseline higher to give the facts in row 12 a full baseline of air.

The facts text runs across columns 1–6 at roughly 55 characters, which is a good measure. Its two lines carry the only serif on the page besides the footer, so the pairing holds. Hang its first baseline exactly on the row 12 top line, where it currently sits half a baseline low.

The photo's blown-out white sky dissolves into the off-white paper along the top of columns 9–12. Crop the image down by about one baseline, or add a 0.5 pt rule along its top edge, so the module edge stays visible.

The green accent appears only in the row 2 label and the single pin. Carry it to a thin rule or tick at the photo's corner on the dot so colour links the map point to the image. Right now the saturated greens of the photo compete with the accent and drown it.
critic.summary: The headline and row structure are strong. The core idea, though, is only asserted by a caption. The pinfield is a small four-column block, and the six-by-four photo does not sit at any map coordinate. Enlarge the map into an underlay, shrink the photo to the exact cell under the Newcastle dot, drop the explanatory note, and tie the green accent to that point.

idea.sentence: Oxford sits inside Oxfordshire as its name sits inside the county's name, so OXFORDSHIRE spans the page, the city hangs beneath the letters OXFORD and the county facts beneath SHIRE.

Most viewers will miss it, though, because all 11 letters are one green. Keep OXFORD green and set SHIRE in the paper-white or grey of the labels, so the 7 | 5 split reads as the idea.

The borders text in columns 8–12 starts in row 9, while the photo in columns 1–7 runs to the end of row 9. Its first line floats about one module above the photo's bottom edge and lines up with nothing. Move it to start in row 10 on the same baseline as the county-town text, so both columns share one text row.

The pinfield is assigned rows 5–8, but the pins drift: the outlying pins at the far left of column 8 drop toward row 9, and the top of the field starts below the photo's top edge. Scale the pins so the cloud fills rows 5–8 from the row-5 hangline. Or extend the field to rows 5–9 so its bottom edge matches the photo's.

Row 12 is empty across all 12 columns, and rows 11–12 under the county-town text form one large dead band. This empty space is not meaningful. Either drop the whole lower block (photo, pinfield, both texts) one row so it rests on row 12, or keep it and move the two text blocks to rows 11–12 so the gap sits between headline and image instead.

The county-town text at roughly 28 pt fills 3 lines across 7 columns and ends on the single word 'settlement.' Rebreak it so the last line holds at least two words. Or narrow the measure to columns 1–6 to tighten the rag and leave column 7 as air beside the pinfield.
The city label and county label share row 4 correctly at columns 1 and 8. The headline sits in rows 2–3 with a full empty row before row 4, which is good separation. Keep this as is.

Color: the green Oxford pin echoing the green headline is the right link between the two columns. The photo's saturated blue sky in rows 5–6 is the loudest thing below the headline. Pull its saturation down slightly so the green stays the only accent.
critic.summary: This is a sound, legible layout. The headline is sized so OXFORD spans exactly 7 columns, which carries the idea. The weak points are the misaligned borders text in row 9, a drifting pinfield, and an unused band in rows 11–12. Differentiating SHIRE by color would make the concept visible. idea.sentence: Warwick lies near the middle of England, so the castle's photo is centred exactly on column 7, row 8, the grid cell that matches its place in the country.

notes: Idea: the geometry is correct. The photo spans columns 4–10, centred on column 7, and rows 6–10, centred on row 8. The reader cannot see that, though. A 12-column grid has no middle column, so the photo sits half a column right of the page axis and reads as a slip, not a map position. Add a small locator in columns 11–12 of row 8: a tiny England outline with a dot, or a mono label such as 'COL 7 · ROW 8'. That one cue turns the offset into the point.

Grid: the photo leaves 3 empty columns on the left (1–3) and 2 on the right (11–12) across rows 6–10. Those leftovers look accidental. Draw a hairline down the centre of column 7 from row 6 to row 10, or a short tick at the top and bottom of the photo, so the off-centre axis is clearly intentional.

Grid: the body starts at column 7, so the photo's axis falls inside the body's first column instead of on its edge. Start the body at column 7 as now, but run a thin vertical rule at the column 7 centre line through row 11. The text block then hangs from the same axis as the photo.

Hierarchy: the sequence works. The headline in columns 1–8 comes first, then the photo, then the lead. 'Warwickshire' in green in row 5 competes as a second headline. Keep its size, but drop the label in row 4 so it shares a baseline with the 'Castle' x-height line. The label then reads as a caption to the headline rather than floating mid-row.

Type: the body in columns 7–12 ends with the single word '1978.' on its own line. Narrow the body to columns 7–11, or adjust tracking, so the last line carries at least two words. Narrowing also brings the line length closer to 55–60 characters.

Type: the lead in columns 1–6 fills both rows 11–12, but the body fills only row 11. Either set the body one step larger so it reaches into row 12, or align the lead's last baseline with the body's last baseline. The two blocks should end on a shared line above the footer rule.

Color: the olive green of 'Warwickshire' picks up the foliage in the photo, and the warm paper suits the stone. Keep this. Do not add a second accent. If you add the locator dot in columns 11–12, row 8, use the same green so the accent marks only the place name and the place.
