idea.sentence: Mathon is a small village at the eastern edge of a large county, so Herefordshire runs the full width of the page while three small church views, the village and its pin sit beneath it.

notes: The three church photos each span 2 of 12 columns but only 1 row, so they read as thumbnails at 2.2× crop and the numbered boxes cover the subject. Let each photo span 2 columns × 2 rows (rows 4–5) or run all three across columns 1–6 at full row height, and drop the numbered squares.

The pinfield claims columns 7–12, rows 4–11, but its dots spill left to about column 6 (the strays at rows 10–11 sit under the body text column edge). Clip the field to columns 7–12, or start it at column 8 so one empty column separates the map from the text.

The red Mathon pin sits mid-field in row 8 and nothing ties it to the left column. Align the place-label or the east-label to the pin's row (move the east-label from row 9 up to row 8) so the eye travels across the page from text to dot.

The place-label in row 5 sits directly under the photos with no air, then row 8 is left empty between the lead and the east-label. Move the place-label up into the lower baseline of row 4's gutter, or shift the lead up one row to 5–6 so the empty row lands as a deliberate pause before the east section.

The lead at roughly 28 pt spans 6 columns with a ragged 3-line block, which is fine, but the body below also spans 6 columns at about 15 pt, giving 50+ character lines next to an empty row 12. Narrow the body to columns 1–5 and keep it on rows 10–11.

The headline fills columns 1–12 as stated but its light weight and tight tracking nearly crowd the right margin; set the final E's right edge exactly on column 12's edge and confirm the cap height lands on a baseline of row 3.
Rows 11–12 under the body and pinfield are empty on the left. That is acceptable, but then remove the stray dots at rows 10–11 in columns 6–7 so the emptiness reads as intended rather than leftover.

Color: the single red accent on the pin and place-label works, but the saturated blue skies of the photos compete with it. Desaturate or warm the photos slightly so the red Mathon pin stays the only strong hue below the headline.
critic.summary: A clear idea — the county spans the full 12 columns and Mathon is a single red dot at its eastern edge — but the execution under the headline is loose. The photos are too small at 2 columns × 1 row, the pinfield leaks past column 7, and the pin is not linked to any text row. Fix the photo spans, contain the map, and align a label to the pin to make this keepable.

copy.text: A small village in eastern Herefordshire, just west of the Malvern Hills.
Mathon lies between Malvern and Ledbury, near Cradley and Colwall. Immediately to the east is the county boundary with Worcestershire.

idea.sentence: York lies north and east of England's centre, so the photograph of its medieval street hangs where York falls on the grid, centred on column 8, row 5, and a small map of Dan's pins beside it shows the same position.

notes: Idea: the photo spans columns 6–10 and rows 3–7, which centres it exactly on column 8, row 5. That mechanic is sound. The locator does not prove it, though. Scale the pinfield up to fill its full columns 1–5 × rows 6–7 block so the cluster reads as England. Then the red York pin can sit visibly north and east of the field's centre, mirroring the photo's offset on the full grid.

Locator: the pins occupy only about columns 3–5 of their 5-column span, and the red York pin floats near the top of row 6. Either align the red pin to the horizontal centre line of row 5, the photo's centre row, by moving the locator up one row into rows 5–6, or draw a thin hairline from the pin to the photo's left edge at column 6. Either way, the link between map and photo becomes explicit.

Grid: the columns 11–12 empty in rows 2–7 are doing real work, because they push the photo east, so keep them. Row 8 is empty between photo and headline, which is good. But row 12 is also left empty under the body text, and the composition sags into the footer. Either bring both body columns down so they hang from the top of row 11 and fill into row 12, or leave them and shorten the gap by moving the headline to rows 9–10 with its baseline on the last baseline of row 10. Right now it floats mid-row.

Hierarchy: the lead in columns 1–5, rows 3–4, is set roughly two steps too large. Its four lines compete with the photo for second place. Drop it one size so it fits in 3 lines within rows 3–4. That leaves the reading order clear: headline, then photo, then lead, then body.

Hierarchy: the place label sits alone in row 2, a full row above the photo. Move it to the last baseline of row 2 so it hangs directly on the photo's top edge at column 6 and reads as the photo's caption rather than a stray line.

Type: the body columns (5 columns each, about 45–50 characters per line) have a good measure and a decent rag. Keep them. The headline spanning all 12 columns at a single light weight is strong. Check that its left stem optically aligns to the column 1 edge, since the 'T' crossbar appears slightly inset.

Color: the red accent appears in only two places, the label in row 2 and the York pin in row 6. That restraint is right, and the red shirts in the photo echo it. Don't add more red; just make sure the pin and label use the identical red value.
critic.summary: The geography-as-grid idea is genuinely good, and the photo's placement on column 8, row 5 executes it precisely. The weak link is the locator: it is too small, sits in the wrong row to echo the photo, and doesn't read as England. Enlarge the locator and align it to row 5, shrink the lead one step, and tighten rows 11–12 to get this to a keeper.

copy.text:
A narrow medieval street in York,
once the Great Flesh Shambles.
Timber-framed buildings with jettied floors overhang the street by several feet. In 1885 thirty-one butchers' shops stood here; none remain today.
York, the traditional county town of Yorkshire, is a cathedral city at the confluence of the rivers Ouse and Foss. It lies 207 miles north of London.

idea.sentence: The teahouse is small and leans while Windsor is the name to learn, so the town spans all twelve columns and the house sits small in the corner beneath it.

notes: The idea says the house sits small in the corner, but the photo spans 4 of 12 columns and 5 rows (8–12), the largest image block on the page. To make 'small' read, cut it to 3 columns × 3 rows (columns 1–3, rows 10–12) so it reads as a corner inset beneath the 12-column WINDSOR.

'Crooked House' at columns 6–11 is the second-loudest element and competes with WINDSOR. Drop it about 40% in size so it fits rows 6–7 as a single row of type, or set it on one line. That keeps the town as the clear dominant and the place as a subordinate name.

The lean is the house's story, but nothing on the grid leans or breaks. Consider shifting the photo off-axis by half a module, or hanging it from row 8 so it overlaps the column-5 gutter. Alternatively, let the photo start at column 2 so it sits visibly off the column-1 margin and echoes the slant.

Rows 4–5 across columns 5–12 and row 5 across columns 1–12 are empty. The gap between the county label (row 4) and Crooked House (row 6) reads as dead space rather than a deliberate pause. Either move the place block up to rows 5–6, or tighten WINDSOR to row 2 and push the county label into row 3 so the empty modules gather into one intentional field below.

The lead in rows 8–9 sits immediately under the place headline with almost no row gap. Meanwhile the body in rows 10–11 floats a full row below the lead. Give one empty half-row between headline and lead, and pull the body up to start on row 10's first baseline, so the right-hand stack spaces evenly.
The body line length runs across 6 columns (~75 characters) at small size. Narrow it to columns 6–10 (5 of 12) for a shorter measure and a better rag. It will also align with the narrower lead line.

The photo's bottom edge sits flush on the footer rule at row 12 while the text column ends at row 11. Either end the body on row 12 to share the photo's baseline, or lift the photo to end on row 11 so both columns close on the same row line.

Color: warm grey paper and black type are fine, but the photo's teal-green trim is the only accent and goes unused. Pull that green into the county label in row 4 or the small index marker, so paper, photo and accent tie together.
critic.summary: A clean, readable layout with a strong 12-column WINDSOR, but it undercuts its own idea. The 'small' house is a large 4×5 photo, and the 'Crooked House' headline competes with the town name. Shrink the photo to a true corner inset, quiet the place headline, tighten the vertical spacing in rows 4–11, and find a grid gesture for the lean.

copy.text:
England’s oldest teahouse,
on “an outrageous slant.”
Dating from c. 1687, reconstructed in the 17th century and Grade II listed. Three storeys, with bay windows to the front and rear.

versions.feedback: Use the attached photo of the Haçienda interior as the main image, large.

idea.sentence: The club itself is gone, so its name fills the top of the page and the lower half places it among Dan's other Greater Manchester pins, listed by distance.

notes: The headline spans 12 of 12 columns across rows 2–4, which carries the 'the name fills the top' idea well. Row 5 is left empty beneath it, and that gap reads as an accidental hole between headline and map. Either push the headline down so its baseline sits on the row 4/5 boundary, or start the pinfield and the nearby-label in row 5 so the lower half begins directly under the name.

The pinfield fills columns 1–6, but its dots cluster in columns 3–5. The empty modules at its left and right edges therefore look like slack rather than intent. Scale the pinfield so the outermost pins touch column 1 and column 6, or reduce its span to columns 2–6 and align its left edge with the header's second field.

The nearby-list occupies rows 7–8 and the body occupies rows 11–12, leaving rows 9–10 of columns 8–12 empty. That leaves a dead block in the right half while the pinfield runs on through row 10. Move the body up to rows 9–10 so the right column ends with the pinfield. Rows 11–12 then become a shared empty band above the footer.

The nearby-label in row 6 sits a full row above the list in row 7. Label and list read as two separate items. Set the label on the last baseline of row 6, directly above item 01, or move the list up into row 6 under the label.

The map-caption in row 11 floats one row below the pinfield, while the body sits on the same row in columns 8–12. Align the caption's top baseline with the body's first line, which it nearly does now, or attach the caption to the last baseline of row 10 so it clearly belongs to the map.

The red Haçienda pin sits around the row 7/8 boundary, level with the list. Its marker is a filled dot over open rings that read as smudged. Use one clean marker with a single ring. Consider drawing a thin hairline from it toward column 8 to tie the pin to the list's distances.

Red is used only for the label and the pin, which is correct, but the accent is too small to register against the warm grey paper. Set the nearby-label one size larger, or make the pin marker two modules of dot size larger, so the red reads as a pairing rather than a speck.
The body measure across columns 8–12 breaks to a one-word last line ('years.'). Rebreak the text or widen the body to columns 7–12 to avoid the widow and get a steadier rag.
critic.summary: The name spanning all 12 columns makes a strong top half, and the pins-by-distance idea comes through. The lower half, however, leaves unplanned empty rows: row 5 across the page, and rows 9–10 in columns 8–12. The label, list and caption also float a row away from what they describe. Tighten the vertical rhythm so the right column ends with the pinfield, and strengthen the red link between pin and list.

copy.text: A nightclub and music venue run by Factory Records, famous during the Madchester years.

idea.sentence: The wall runs across the whole width of the island, so the county name runs across the whole width of the page and the wall sits beneath it, edge to edge.

notes: The headline spans 12 of 12 columns but stops short of the right margin by roughly half a column; track or scale it so the final D lands exactly on the column 12 edge, otherwise the 'edge to edge' idea reads as approximate.

The headline sits in rows 2–3 but its cap height fills only the top of row 2 and the start of row 3, leaving nearly a full empty row above the photo. Either drop the headline so its baseline sits on the last baseline of row 3, or pull the photo up into row 3's lower module so headline and wall touch as the idea demands.

The photo spans columns 1–12 and rows 4–9, which is right for the idea. Crop it so the wall line runs more horizontally across the 12 columns rather than diagonally into the right corner; the current crop makes the wall recede instead of spanning.

The place-label wraps to two lines in a 3-column span ('BARDON / MILL'). Widen it to columns 1–3 with tighter tracking, or set it on one line by shortening to a 3-column measure. Hang its first baseline on the same baseline as the lead's first line in row 10.

The lead spans 9 columns at a large size and gives three lines with a hyphen break at 'Bowness-on-'. Reduce the span to columns 4–11 or adjust the size so 'Bowness-on-Solway' stays unbroken and the rag improves.

The body sits alone in row 12 with an empty module between it and the lead in row 11. Move it up to start in the lower half of row 11 so lead and body read as one block. Set it to columns 4–9 (6 of 12) so the 9-column measure stops producing a ~90-character line.

The pinfield in columns 1–3, rows 11–12 floats with no clear anchor. Align its top dot to the first baseline of row 11 and its left edge to column 1. Add a scale or line hint so the dots read as the wall's position across the island.
The green accent of the headline matches the photo's foliage well. Repeat it only on the highlighted pin, as now, and keep the body in the darker grey so it does not compete.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea: a full-width headline over a full-width wall photo. Execution is loose, though. The headline doesn't truly reach column 12, an empty row floats between headline and photo, and the lower text block has a gap at row 11 plus an over-long body measure. Tighten the headline-to-photo contact, fix the label wrap and lead hyphenation, and pull the body up onto a 6-column measure.

copy.text: Begun in AD 122, the stone wall ran from Wallsend on the River Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway, across the whole width of the island.
Bardon Mill is a small village near the wall, 32 mi from Newcastle upon Tyne and 26½ mi from Carlisle.

idea.sentence: The Lovell Telescope is best understood by walking towards it, so one photo of its focus tower steps across the grid three times, each larger and closer.

notes: The 2→4→6 column and 2→4→6 row progression is a real step and reads correctly. But all three photos hang from the top of row 4, so they grow downward and read like a falling stair, not an approach. Bottom-align them on row 9 instead: far in rows 8–9, nearer in rows 6–9, close in rows 4–9. They then stand on a shared ground line and rise as you walk closer.

Once the photos are bottom-aligned, columns 1–6 open up in rows 4–5 (above nearer) and rows 4–7 (above far). Move the lead into columns 1–6, rows 4–5. The lead then sits directly under the headline, and the photo band closes the composition at row 9.

Rows 11–12 sit almost entirely empty across all 12 columns. Only two lines of body poke into row 11, so the lower quarter reads as leftover rather than chosen space. Either drop body to rows 11–12 so its last line lands on the bottom of row 12, or tighten the photo band and let row 12 be a clean, full-width empty row.

Keep the place label on row 10 in columns 7–12, hanging on the same baseline as the first line of body; that cross-alignment is good. Start it at the left edge of column 7, flush with close photo 3, as it does now. Don't indent it.

The lead runs to three lines in a 6-column measure and leaves a ragged gap before row 10. Set it so it fills exactly rows 8–9, or rows 4–5 if you move it. Two lines on four baselines each would let its last baseline lock to the row line.

The headline's light weight at full 12-column span is right. Its left side bearing on the J sits slightly inside column 1's edge, so optically nudge it to align with the photo edge below. The lead/body size jump is clear, and the mono label is a good third voice.

The blue place label picks up the sky in all three photos, so the single accent is well chosen. Keep it the only coloured type. The white number boxes 1–3 sit at the bottom-left module of each photo; keep them one consistent distance from the photo corner, as they nearly are.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea executed with a disciplined 2/4/6 module progression and restrained type and colour. The main weakness is the top alignment, which makes the photos grow downward instead of approaching. That leaves the lower rows 11–12 as unplanned empty space. Bottom-align the stair on row 9 and move the lead up into the space this frees.

copy.text: Established in 1945 by Bernard Lovell to investigate cosmic rays.
The observatory tracked Soviet and US spacecraft of the Space Race. The Lovell Radio Telescope is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

idea.sentence: The chapel is a commonly used symbol of its city, so the name Cambridge fills the page and the chapel sits beneath it.

notes: The headline spans all 12 columns across rows 2–4, which delivers 'the name fills the page'. But the photo sits beside the text, in columns 7–12, rather than 'beneath' the name. To make the stated relationship literal, start the photo in row 5 directly under the 'bridge' letters and let it run to row 11, so the chapel hangs from the word.

Row 4 below the descender of 'g' is almost empty, so the headline floats a full module above the content block. Either push the headline down so its baseline sits on the row 4 line, or start the county label and the photo in row 4 to close the gap.

The left text column spans 5 columns (1–5) while the photo starts at column 7, leaving column 6 as an orphan gutter. Widen the text block to columns 1–6 so the two halves split cleanly 6/6, or narrow the text to 1–4 and give column 5–6 as deliberate air.

Row 8 is empty between the lead (rows 6–7) and the body (rows 9–10). The jump reads as arbitrary rather than structural. Align the body's last line with the photo's bottom edge on row 10 so the gap becomes a hanging alignment, which it nearly is now; make it exact on the baseline.

The 'On the River Cam' label sits alone in row 12, columns 1–5, disconnected from everything. Move it to row 11 directly under the photo in columns 7–12 as a caption, or drop it. Row 11 is currently dead across all 12 columns.

The lead at roughly 28 pt over 5 columns gives about 25 characters per line, which works. The body is in grey at about 16 pt and is close in size to the lead. Drop the body to 11–12 pt on the 12 pt baseline so the three steps (headline, lead, body) read as distinct.
The warm photo and the tinted brown county label pair well with the off-white paper. Keep the accent to that label only; the grey body text slightly muddies it, so set the body in black.
critic.summary: A clean, competent layout with a strong full-width headline. The stated idea, though, says the chapel sits beneath the name, while the grid places it beside the text. The block of rows 5–12 has loose vertical rhythm: rows 8 and 11 are empty without purpose, and a lone label sits in row 12. Tighten the photo to sit directly under the headline, square the 5+1+6 column split, and turn the stray label into a caption.

copy.text: King's College Chapel features the world's largest fan vault.
Built in phases by a succession of kings of England from 1448 to 1515. Its large stained glass windows were completed by 1531.

idea.sentence: Boscastle lies at the far south-western corner of England, so the photo drops to the bottom-left of the grid, just where Cornwall sits on the map, and the rest of the page stays open like the country to the north and east.

notes: The map idea only half-reads: the photo in columns 1–4, rows 8–12 sits bottom-left, but the 12-column headline across rows 2–4 fills the 'north' and the lead in columns 7–12 fills the 'east'. To make the page read as open country, pull the lead down so its top aligns with row 8 and leave columns 5–12 of rows 5–7 empty.

Row 5 is an empty band between the headline and the label/lead pair. It looks like leftover space rather than a chosen gap. Either commit to the openness by moving the label and lead down one row, or start them in row 5.
The county label in columns 1–4, row 6 floats alone over five empty rows. Hang it from the top of row 8 directly above the photo, so it captions Cornwall's corner rather than drifting in the field.

The lead spans 6 columns at a large size and sets four lines across rows 6–7, about 35 characters per line. That is fine. But its first baseline sits lower than the cap height of the county label beside it. Align the label's cap height to the lead's first line, or separate the two by a full row.

The body spans only 3 columns (5–7) and gives a choppy rag of about 22 characters per line ('folk / magic, ceremonial / magic'). Widen it to 4 columns (5–8) to match the photo-label and harbour-label above and below it. That gives one consistent text column.

The body starts mid-row 9, leaving a visible gap under the photo-label in row 8. Snap the body's first baseline to the top of row 9, or tuck it directly under the label in row 8, so the column reads as one stack.

The harbour-label in row 12 breaks after 'Sir', orphaning 'Richard Grenville'. Widen it to columns 5–9, or break it after '1584' so the name stays whole. Keep its last baseline on the photo's bottom edge.

Columns 9–12 of rows 8–12 are empty. That is good for the idea, but the photo at 4 columns is modest. Try widening it to columns 1–5, with the text column shifted to 6–9, so the southwestern 'weight' is stronger against the open northeast.
Colour works: the brick-red headline picks up the stone arch, and the red photo-label ties back to it. Keep the red to those two uses only.
critic.summary: A calm, competent page whose map metaphor is undercut by the headline and lead filling the north and east. Tighten the text column to one 4-column width aligned to the photo, resolve the dead row 5, and drop the lead lower so the open field is genuinely open.

copy.text: A museum of European witchcraft and magic in a fishing port on the north coast of Cornwall.
Its exhibits cover folk magic, ceremonial magic, Freemasonry and Wicca. The collection has been described as the largest in the world.

idea.sentence: Nothing Dan has saved lies within 5 km of the stones, so that absence becomes the poster's second headline, with the nearest company across Wiltshire listed beneath it.

notes: The gap statement fills only the top half of its rows 5–7 slot in columns 9–12. Rows 6–7 below it are dead space that reads as leftover, not as chosen emptiness. Pull the 'Elsewhere in Wiltshire' label up to row 7 so the absence and the alternative sit as one block. Or keep the gap but move the list down to end on the photo's bottom edge at row 10, so the void is framed on purpose.

The 'Elsewhere in Wiltshire' label in row 8 floats a full module above the list in rows 9–10, which orphans it from what it introduces. Set it one baseline above the first list line, sharing the list's rows.

The list stops about a module short of the photo's bottom edge in row 10, so columns 9–12 and columns 1–8 end on different lines. Hang the last list line on the photo's bottom baseline so the two blocks close together.

'King Alfred's Tower, Stourhead' wraps to a second line inside the 4-column list and breaks the one-place-per-line rhythm. Either drop the distance column to a narrower 1-column slot and give names 3 columns, or shorten the name to 'King Alfred's Tower'.

'within 5 km' runs right up to the edge of column 12 with no air, while 'Nothing' stops near column 11. Drop the size one step so both lines sit inside columns 9–12 with a visible right margin. The headline should still clearly outrank the lead.

The pinfield is meant to show the 5 km absence, but its dots cluster in columns 10–11 and the blue Stonehenge pin is a tangle of overlapping rings. Draw a single empty 5 km circle around one clean blue dot so the empty module carries the idea. Then centre the cluster on column 10–11's midpoint, or align it to the left edge of column 9 to match the list above.

The lead spans columns 1–6 in rows 11–12, but its third line runs into column 7, leaving a ragged right edge that drifts past the 6-column measure. Rebreak the lines so all three stay inside columns 1–6, or widen the slot to a declared 7 columns.

The county label in row 4 sits alone with a large gap before the photo in row 5. That is acceptable, but align its baseline to the top of row 4 so the space under it clearly belongs to the row 4–5 break.
critic.summary: A clear idea with sound top-level structure: a full-width headline, then an 8+4 column split with the photo and the blue absence statement, and the eye moves in the right order. The right-hand column is loosely stacked, though. The gap statement leaves rows 6–7 half-used, the section label floats a module away from its list, and the list doesn't close on the photo's bottom edge. The pinfield is the natural place to make the 5 km emptiness visible, and right now it is a muddled cluster. Tighten the column 9–12 stack onto shared row lines and draw the empty radius, and this reaches a keeper.

copy.text: A prehistoric ring of sarsen stones on Salisbury Plain, two miles west of Amesbury.

idea.sentence: The castle sits inside a storybook town, so three views step down and across the grid, each larger and closer: the town from the air, then the quadrangle and its walls, then the keep on its motte.

notes: The staircase works: view 1 spans 4 columns over 2 rows, view 2 spans 6 columns over 3 rows, view 3 spans 8 columns over 4 rows. The left edges step 1, 3, 5, so each image moves two columns right as it grows. Keep this progression. To make it read as one diagonal, end view 2 at column 8 so its right edge touches the column view 3 starts at (5). Better still, move view 2 to columns 3–8 and view 3 to 7–12 so all three steps are equal.

View 3 is image 4 cropped at 2.2×, the same source as view 2. The idea promises three distinct views, but the keep shot repeats the quadrangle photo, enlarged. Either use a separate keep photograph in columns 5–12, rows 9–12, or crop tighter on the motte so the zoom reads as intended rather than duplicated.

The headline spans 9 of 12 columns across rows 2–3, and the category label floats at columns 10–12 on row 3. Drop the label to sit on the headline's baseline at the bottom of row 3 rather than mid-cap-height, so the two share a line.

The lead in columns 6–11, rows 4–5 sets at 3 lines and leaves column 12 and part of row 5 empty. Start it at column 6 to align with view 3's start at column 5 instead, or move it to columns 5–10. Then the text column and the large photo share one vertical edge and the right side is not a sixth unrelated axis.

The body sits in columns 9–12 on row 8, hanging off view 2's bottom right. Align its last baseline to view 2's bottom edge, which it nearly does. Also widen it to start at column 9's left edge exactly, since it currently reads indented a few points.

The pinfield fills columns 1–4, rows 9–11, but its dots cluster in columns 2–3, leaving column 1 and the top of row 9 visually empty. Either scale the field to the full 4-column width or give it a frame so it reads as a module and not scatter. The county label on row 12 is correctly placed under it.

Hierarchy runs headline, then the large keep, then the lead, so the eye jumps from the top straight to the bottom right. Step the lead up a size or tighten the top block so the aerial view and lead read as one unit before the descent begins.

Colour is sound: the olive #344618 headline echoes the lawns in all three photos, and the red #C8102E is held to the label, the number boxes and the pin. Keep the red that sparse; the number boxes could drop their dark fill for paper so the red outline carries alone.
critic.summary: A clear, worthwhile idea: three photos stepping down and across the grid, each two columns wider. The grid largely delivers it. To make it publishable, fix the repeated source image in view 3, align the lead's left edge to the photo columns, and make the right edges of the staircase step evenly so the diagonal is exact.

Damaged in the English Civil War, it was restored by the 11th Duke of Norfolk.

idea.sentence: Tintagel lies near the narrow south-western tip of England, so its photo is a small point in the lowest left-hand cells, with the open left side standing for the sea around Cornwall.

notes: Idea: the small photo in columns 1–2, rows 11–12 does read as a point at the lower left, but columns 1–4 are empty from row 2 to row 9 with nothing to say 'sea'. Either let the photo be the only thing in columns 1–4 and move the 'Cornwall' label into row 12 under it, or shift the photo one column further left by bleeding it to the margin so it reads as the tip of the land, not a stray thumbnail.

Grid: the headline and lead both hang from column 5 and the body splits 5–8 / 9–12, which is clean. Rows 8–10 are empty across columns 5–12. That gap is three full rows, so the lead floats. Move the lead down to rows 7–8 so the empty band shrinks to rows 9–10 and the page reads as two blocks, top and bottom.

Grid: the 'Cornwall' label sits in row 10 while the photo starts in row 11, leaving almost a full row between label and image. Move the label to the last baseline of row 10, or into the top of row 11 with the photo dropped one baseline, so the caption touches its picture.

Grid: the photo spans columns 1–2 and stops at the bottom of row 12, but the body text in columns 5–12 sets only three to four lines from the top of row 11. Align the first body baseline with the photo's top edge and let the body columns hang from the same line. They already nearly do, so lock them to the row 11 top baseline.

Hierarchy: headline, then lead, then body reads correctly. The photo at 2 of 12 columns is so small it drops below the body in weight. That suits the idea, but give it a clearer edge. Either crop it tighter to the bridge or lift its contrast so the point is legible at that size.

Type: the lead at roughly 3 baselines per line over 8 columns runs about 45 characters, which is fine. Its line 'Island, beside the village of Tintagel on' ends on 'on' and makes a weak rag. Rebreak so 'on' moves to line 3. The body in 4-column measures is good. Tighten the headline's line gap by one baseline so 'Castle' sits closer to 'Tintagel'.

Type: the lead is set in the same blue and a heavy-ish weight close to the headline, so it competes. Drop it to regular weight, or set it in black at the same size, so the headline alone owns the blue.

Color: #012169 is used on both headline and lead, and nothing ties it to the photo. Since the idea is the sea, use the blue once more as a thin rule or field in the empty columns 1–4 near rows 10–12, or keep it only on the headline. Right now the accent spreads over 8 columns at the top and never reaches the left-hand 'sea'.
critic.summary: A tidy, correctly hung layout with a sensible headline–lead–body order. The stated idea of a tiny point at the lower left with open sea around it is only half-delivered: the empty columns 1–4 read as unused rather than as sea. The three-row dead band in rows 8–10 and the loose label above the photo weaken the grid. Close the vertical gaps, fix the lead's rag and weight, and make the blue or the photo carry the sea idea.

copy.text: A medieval fortification on Tintagel Island, beside the village of Tintagel on the Atlantic coast of North Cornwall.

idea.sentence: The castle is small in its moat and the county around it is large, so East Sussex fills the page and Bodiam sits small below it, with open land between.

notes: The idea reads: the headline spans 12 of 12 columns across rows 2–6, the photo holds 4 columns in rows 10–12, and rows 7–9 stay empty as the 'open land'. Keep that empty band. To make the castle feel smaller in its moat, cut the photo to columns 1–3 and rows 11–12 so it is lighter against the 12-column county.

The lead runs columns 7–11 and splits 'Robertsbridge,' / '1385 by Sir Edward' unevenly, leaving a ragged right edge. Widen it to columns 7–12, or step the size down one notch so it sets in 3 lines within rows 11–12 and its last baseline lands on the photo's bottom edge in row 12.

The place-label sits at the top of row 10 while the lead starts low in row 11, leaving a loose gap of about one row between them. Move the label to the last baseline of row 10, or start the lead on the first baseline of row 11, so the label and lead read as one unit.

Columns 5–6 between the photo and the text block are an empty gutter module. That gap separates two halves that belong to the same castle. Either start the label and lead at column 6 to close it, or keep it and align the label's cap height exactly with the photo's top edge in row 10, so the two blocks are tied across the gap.

The headline's 'EAST' ends near column 8 and 'SUSSEX' fills to column 12. That is fine, but the S of 'SUSSEX' optically overhangs the column 1 edge. Nudge it so the stems of E and S align on column 1.

Colour: the navy #012169 appears only in the headline and the label. The photo's warm stone and pink sky sit apart from it. Consider keeping the label black so the navy belongs only to the county, which strengthens the county-versus-castle contrast.
critic.summary: This poster is a clear, honest take on the idea: a full-width county, an empty band across rows 7–9, and a small castle below. The lower zone needs tightening. Shrink the photo to 3 columns, set the lead cleanly across columns 7–12 aligned to the photo base, and close the gap between the label and the lead.

idea.sentence: Abbey Road is one stop on a short London walk, so the studio sits above a list of its nearest pins and a map dot showing where it falls in Greater London.

notes: The headline is set across all 12 columns, but its glyphs end around the top third of row 4. The rest of row 4 is a dead strip above the photo. Either scale the headline so its descenders sit on the row 4 baseline, or end the headline at row 3 and start the photo and lead at row 4. That moves the whole middle band up one module and frees row 9 for breathing room.

The nearby-list is allotted rows 11–12, but its three lines sit at the very bottom of row 11. That leaves an empty module between the 'Nearby pins' label in row 10 and the list. Hang the list from the top of row 11 so the label and list read as one unit, and let the leftover space fall to row 12.

The distances are right-aligned at the edge of column 7, while the names end around column 4. That leaves a 3-column gap the eye has to jump across. Narrow the list to columns 1–5, with names in columns 1–4 and km right-aligned in column 5. Columns 6–7 become an intentional empty module under the photo's right edge.

The 'Greater London' label starts at column 9, but the pin cloud floats in columns 10–11 and is centred vertically in rows 11–12. Left-align the pinfield's bounding box to column 9 and top-align it to row 11 so map and label share an edge. Then scale the field to fill columns 9–12: at the current size the dots are specks and the red Abbey Road dot reads as a blot.

Column 8 is empty in rows 10–12 but filled by the lead in rows 5–8. That shifts the lower band's right-hand start from column 8 to column 9 for no reason. Start the county-label and pinfield at column 8 to match the lead above (columns 8–12), so the right side keeps one vertical edge from row 5 to row 12.

The lead runs about 28 pt across 5 columns, giving 5 lines that fill rows 6–8. The rag is decent, but 'Road,' pushes almost to the column 12 edge while 'established in' leaves a deep hole. Drop the lead one size so it sits in rows 6–7 at roughly 4 lines, with a smoother rag. Row 8 then becomes the empty module that separates it from the photo's bottom.

The place-label in row 5 aligns to the top of the photo, which is good. But the lead starts a full module lower, so the label floats. Either set the lead on the row 5 baseline directly under the label, with one baseline between them, or move the label down to sit on the lead.

The small red numbered square in the bottom-left corner of the photo (column 1, row 9) is a fifth use of the accent. It reads as a stray mark on the car. Remove it, or tie it explicitly to the '01–03' numbering system. Keep red to the place-label, list numerals and the map dot.

The idea is 'one stop on a walk', but nothing shows sequence or route. The list is just three distances and the map is a scatter. Give the list a 'previous / next stop' framing, or draw the walk line in the pinfield across columns 8–12. That way the lower band, rows 10–12, earns the walk concept instead of reading as generic metadata.
critic.summary: This is a clean, mostly well-ordered poster with a strong 12-column headline and a solid photo-and-lead pair in rows 5–9. The lower band (rows 10–12) is the weak part. The list sits a module low and is spread too wide across 7 columns. The pinfield is undersized and off the column 9 edge, and column 8 breaks the right-hand alignment set by the lead. Tighten those spans and pull the headline gap out of row 4, and this reaches a keepable 7 across the board.

idea.sentence: Holy Island lies at the very top of England, so the castle hangs from the top row of the page, on the same line as its pin on the map.

notes: Idea: the Holy Island pin sits roughly on the photo's top edge in row 2, so the link is there, but it reads as coincidence. Snap the pin's centre exactly to the photo's top edge at the top of row 2. Then run a hairline in #495516 from the pin across columns 4–6 to the photo, so the 'hanging' is visible rather than implied.

Pinfield: the dots only occupy roughly columns 2–5 of the 6-column span, and the lowest stray dot falls into row 6 beside the label. Scale the map so the field fills columns 1–6 edge to edge and ends at the bottom of row 5 with the photo. Row 6 then belongs to the label alone.

Highlighted pin: the accent pin is barely larger than the grey dots, so a reader cannot find the point the idea rests on. Enlarge it to about twice the size of the other pins, or keep the other pins at a lighter grey, so it reads first within columns 1–6.

Row 7: this row is fully empty and splits the page into two unrelated halves. Keep it empty, but push the headline up so its cap height starts at the top of row 8 exactly. At present the descender-free word floats with uneven space above (row 7) and below (before row 10).
Lead and causeway: both start in row 10, but their first baselines differ by about one baseline. Hang both first lines on the same baseline at the top of row 10.
Causeway text: this block ends on the single word 'causeway.' Narrow it to columns 7–10, or rewrap it to two full lines, to remove the widow and give a firmer rag.

Row 12: the 'Also in Northumberland' label in columns 1–3 sits one baseline above the first list item in columns 4–12. Align the label's baseline with item 01. Also pull the distances in from column 12 to column 9, so the eye does not cross five empty columns to read '8.2 km'.
Type pairing: the condensed grotesk headline, the serif text and the mono labels work well together. Keep the lead at three lines across 6 columns; its measure is good.
Colour: the olive accent picks up the grass in the photo and ties the place label, the pin and the list numbers together. Keep it, but use it only on those three so it stays a signal.
critic.summary: A clean, well-proportioned poster with a strong full-width headline and a coherent palette. The stated idea, though, depends on a pin that is too small and an alignment to the photo top that is only approximate. Make the pin-to-photo relationship exact and visible, tighten the pinfield to its 6-column span, and fix the baseline mismatches in rows 10 and 12, and it is ready to keep.
